stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 1
summaryBullets: In the second year of the reign of Artaxerxes the Great, on the first day of Nisan, Mordecai son of Jair son of Shimei son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, had a dream. (1:2).
He was a Jew living in the city of Susa, a great man serving in the court of the king. (1:3).
He was one of the captives whom King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had taken captive from Jerusalem with King Jeconiah of Judea. And this was his dream: (1:4).
Noises and confusion, thunder and earthquake, tumult on the earth! (1:5).
Then two great dragons came forward, both ready to fight, and they roared terribly. (1:6).
At their roaring every nation prepared for war, to fight against a nation of righteous people. (1:7).
It was a day of darkness and gloom, of tribulation and distress, affliction and great tumult on the earth! (1:8).
And the whole righteous nation was troubled; they feared the evils that threatened them and were ready to perish. (1:9).
Then they cried out to God, and at their outcry, as though from a tiny spring, there came a great river with abundant water; (1:10).
light came, and the sun rose, and the lowly were exalted and devoured those held in honor. (1:11).
Mordecai saw in this dream what God had determined to do, and after he awoke he had it on his mind, seeking all day to understand it in every detail. (1:12).
crossRefs: Genesis 41:1–32: Dreams as divine foreshadowing.
Daniel 2:28: God reveals mysteries.
Esther 6:1–3: Mordecai’s loyalty remembered later.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּנִּין (tannîn, 'dragon/serpent'), Greek: δράκοντες (drákontes), Aramaic: תניניא (tannīnyā)
translationNotes.note: Symbolic figures representing opposing forces in Mordecai’s vision, later understood as Haman and Mordecai.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai’s dream foreshadows Israel’s coming danger and deliverance, and his loyalty to the king is established.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 2
summaryBullets: Now Mordecai took his rest in the courtyard with Gabatha and Tharra, the two eunuchs of the king who kept watch in the courtyard. (2:1).
He overheard their conversation and inquired into their purposes and learned that they were preparing to lay hands on King Artaxerxes, and he informed the king concerning them. (2:2).
Then the king examined the two eunuchs, and after they had confessed it, they were led away. (2:3).
The king wrote these things down as a commemoration, and Mordecai wrote an account of them. (2:4).
And the king ordered Mordecai to serve in the court and rewarded him for these things. (2:5).
But Haman son of Hammedatha, a Bougean, who was in great honor with the king, determined to injure Mordecai and his people because of the two eunuchs of the king. (2:6).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 19:11-12: Loyalty that warns the king of a plot.
Proverbs 25:13: A faithful messenger refreshes his masters.
2 Kings 11:14-16: Conspirators inside the royal court.

translationNotes.original: Greek: εὐνοῦχοι (eunouchoi); Hebrew background: סָרִיס (sārîs), a chamber officer.
translationNotes.note: Persian court eunuchs held trusted positions near the throne; their conspiracy here parallels the later canonical account of Bigthan and Teresh (Esther 2:21-23 MT).

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai overhears a plot by two royal eunuchs against King Artaxerxes and reports it; his loyalty is rewarded, while Haman quietly resolves to harm him because of it.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 3
summaryBullets: It was after this that the following things happened in the days of Artaxerxes, the same Artaxerxes who ruled over one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. (3:1).
In those days, when King Artaxerxes was enthroned in the city of Susa, (3:2).
in the third year of his reign, he gave a banquet for his Friends and other persons of various nations, the Persians and Median nobles, and the governors of the satrapies. (3:3).
After this, when he had displayed to them the riches of his kingdom and the splendor of his bountiful celebration during the course of one hundred eighty days, (3:4).
at the end of the wedding feast the king gave a drinking party for the people of various nations who lived in the city. This was held for six days in the courtyard of the royal palace, (3:5).

which was adorned with curtains of fine linen and cotton, held by cords of linen and purple fabric attached to gold and silver blocks on pillars of marble and other stones. Gold and silver couches were placed on a mosaic floor of emerald, mother-of-pearl, and marble. There were coverings of gauze, embroidered in various colors, with roses scattered around them. (3:6).
The cups were of gold and silver, and a miniature cup was displayed, made of ruby, worth thirty thousand talents. There was abundant sweet wine, such as the king himself drank. (3:7).
This drinking party was not in accordance with established custom, but the king wished to have it so, and he commanded his stewards to comply with his pleasure and with that of the guests. (3:8).
Meanwhile, Queen Vashti gave a drinking party for the women in the palace where King Artaxerxes was. (3:9).
On the seventh day, when the king was in good humor, he told Haman, Bazan, Tharra, Boraze, Zatholtha, Abataza, and Tharaba, the seven eunuchs who served King Artaxerxes, (3:10).

to escort the queen to him in order to proclaim her as queen and to place the diadem on her head and to have her display her beauty to all the governors and the people of various nations, for she was indeed a beautiful woman. (3:11).
But Queen Vashti refused to obey him and would not come with the eunuchs. This offended the king, and he became furious. (3:12).
He said to his Friends, “This is how Vashti has answered me. Give, therefore, your ruling and judgment on this matter.” (3:13).
Arkesaeus, Sarsathaeus, and Malesear, the governors of the Persians and Medes who were closest to the king, who sat beside him in the chief seats, came to him (3:14).
and told him what, according to the law, was to be done to Queen Vashti for not obeying the order that the king had sent her by the eunuchs. (3:15).
crossRefs: Ezra 9:6–15: Confession of national sin.
Daniel 9:4–19: Prayer of intercession in exile.
Hebrews 4:16: Approach God’s throne with boldness.

translationNotes.original: Greek: Ἀρταξέρξης (Artaxerxes); Persian: Khshayarsha, ruling 127 provinces from India (Ἰνδική) to Ethiopia (Αἰθιοπία).
translationNotes.note: The Greek Esther names Artaxerxes where the Hebrew names Ahasuerus; the LXX recasts the king under a more familiar Greek dynastic name.

stories.keyTakeaway: Artaxerxes hosts a vast banquet displaying the wealth of his empire; on the seventh day he commands Queen Vashti to appear before his guests, and her refusal triggers the king's fury and a search for legal recourse.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 4
summaryBullets: After these things, the king’s anger abated, and he no longer remembered Vashti or remembered what he had said and how he had condemned her. (4:1).
Then the king’s servants said, “Let beautiful and virtuous young women be sought out for the king. (4:2).

The king shall appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, and they shall select beautiful young virgins to be brought to the harem in the city of Susa. Let them be entrusted to the king’s eunuch who is in charge of the women, and let ointments and whatever else they need be given them. (4:3).
And the woman who pleases the king shall be queen instead of Vashti.” This pleased the king, and he did so. (4:4).
Now there was a Jew in the city of Susa whose name was Mordecai son of Jair son of Shimei son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin; (4:5).
he had been taken captive from Jerusalem among those whom King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had captured. (4:6).

And he had a foster child, the daughter of his father’s brother, Aminadab, and her name was Esther. When her parents died, he brought her up as a wife for himself. The young woman was beautiful in appearance. (4:7).
So when the decree of the king was proclaimed and many young women were gathered in the city of Susa in custody of Gai, Esther also was brought to Gai, who had custody of the women. (4:8).

The young woman pleased him and won his favor, and he quickly provided her with ointments and her portion of food, as well as seven young women chosen from the palace; he treated her and her maids with special favor in the harem. (4:9).
Now Esther had not disclosed her people or country, for Mordecai had commanded her not to make it known. (4:10).
And every day Mordecai walked in the courtyard of the harem, to see what would happen to Esther. (4:11).

Now the period after which a young woman was to go to the king was twelve months. During this time the days of cosmetic treatment are completed: six months while they are anointing themselves with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and ointments for women. (4:12).
Then she goes in to the king; she is handed to the person appointed and goes with him from the harem to the king’s palace. (4:13).

In the evening she enters, and in the morning she departs to the second harem, where Gai the king’s eunuch is in charge of the women, and she does not go in to the king again unless she is summoned by name. (4:14).

When the time was fulfilled for Esther daughter of Aminadab, the brother of Mordecai’s father, to go in to the king, she neglected none of the things that the eunuch in charge of the women had commanded. For Esther found favor in the eyes of all who saw her. (4:15).
So Esther went in to King Artaxerxes in the twelfth month, which is Adar, in the seventh year of his reign. (4:16).
And the king loved Esther passionately, and she found favor beyond all the other virgins, and he put on her the queen’s diadem. (4:17).
crossRefs: Genesis 39:21: Joseph found favor in foreign service.
Daniel 1:9: God grants favor to his exiles before pagan officials.
1 Samuel 16:7: The Lord chooses according to the heart.

translationNotes.original: Greek: θυγάτηρ θετή (thygatēr thetē, 'adopted daughter'); the Hebrew has בַּת־דֹּדוֹ (bat-dōdô, 'cousin').
translationNotes.note: The LXX reads that Mordecai raised Esther 'as a wife for himself,' a unique Greek variant softened in many later traditions; the Hebrew simply says he raised her as his own daughter.

stories.keyTakeaway: After the king's officers gather beautiful young women from across the empire, Esther wins favor in the harem and is brought before Artaxerxes; he loves her above all the others and sets the queen's diadem on her head.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 5
summaryBullets: After these events King Artaxerxes honored Haman son of Hammedatha, a Bougean, and exalted him, and would seat him first among all the king’s Friends. (5:1).
So all who were at court used to do obeisance to Haman, for so the king had commanded to be done. Mordecai, however, did not do obeisance. (5:2).
Then the king’s courtiers said to Mordecai, “Mordecai, why do you disobey the king’s command?” (5:3).
Day after day they spoke to him, but he would not listen to them. Then they informed Haman that Mordecai was resisting the king’s command. Mordecai had told them that he was a Jew. (5:4).
So when Haman learned that Mordecai was not doing obeisance to him, he became furiously angry (5:5).
and resolved to destroy all the Jews under Artaxerxes’s rule. (5:6).

In the twelfth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, Haman came to a decision and cast lots, taking the days and the months one by one, to fix on one day to destroy the whole people of Mordecai. The lot fell on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar. (5:7).

Then Haman said to King Artaxerxes, “There is a certain nation scattered among the other nations in all your kingdom; their laws are different from those of every other nation, and they do not keep the laws of the king. It is not expedient for the king to tolerate them. (5:8).
If it pleases the king, let him decree that they are to be destroyed, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the king’s treasury.” (5:9).
So the king took off his signet ring and gave it to Haman to seal the decree that was to be written against the Jews. (5:10).
The king told Haman, “Keep the money, and do whatever you want with that nation.” (5:11).

So on the thirteenth day of the first month the king’s secretaries were summoned, and in accordance with Haman’s instructions they wrote in the name of King Artaxerxes to the magistrates and the governors in every province from India to Ethiopia, one hundred twenty-seven provinces in all, and to the governors of the nations, each in his own language. (5:12).
Instructions were sent by couriers throughout all the empire of Artaxerxes to destroy the Jewish people in a single day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, and to plunder their goods. ——— (5:13).
crossRefs: Genesis 32:11: Jacob fears but prays for deliverance.
Nehemiah 2:1–5: Cupbearer’s fear before the king.
Proverbs 21:1: King’s heart in God’s hand.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שַׁרְבִיט זָהָב (šarbîṭ zahāb), Greek: σκῆπτρον χρυσοῦν (skēptron chrysoûn), Aramaic: שרביטא דדהבא (šarbīṭā d’dahabā)
translationNotes.note: Symbol of royal authority; Esther’s life depended on the king’s gesture of acceptance.

stories.keyTakeaway: Esther risks her life before the king, but God grants her favor as Haman’s plot continues.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 6
summaryBullets: This is a copy of the letter: “The Great King, Artaxerxes, writes the following to the governors of the hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia and to the officials under them: (6:1).

“Having become ruler of many nations and master of the whole world (not elated with presumption of authority but always acting reasonably and with kindness), I have determined to settle the lives of my subjects in lasting tranquility and, in order to make my kingdom peaceable and open to travel throughout all its extent, to restore the peace desired by all people. (6:2).

“When I asked my counselors how this might be accomplished, Haman—who excels among us in sound judgment and is distinguished for his unchanging goodwill and steadfast fidelity and has attained the second place of honor in the kingdom— (6:3).

pointed out to us that among all the nations in the world there is scattered a certain hostile people who have laws contrary to those of every nation and continually disregard the ordinances of kings, so that the unifying of the kingdom that we honorably intend cannot be brought about. (6:4).

We understand that this people, and it alone, stands constantly in opposition to all humanity, perversely following a strange manner of life and laws, and is ill-disposed to our interests, doing all the harm they can so that our kingdom may not attain stability. (6:5).

“Therefore we have decreed that those indicated to you in the letters written by Haman, who is in charge of affairs and is our second father, shall all—wives and children included—be utterly destroyed by the swords of their enemies, without pity or restraint, on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, of this present year, (6:6).
so that those who have long been hostile and remain so may in a single day go down in violence to Hades and leave our interests secure and untroubled hereafter.” (6:7).
crossRefs: Daniel 6:8: A Persian edict, once sealed, cannot be revoked.
Proverbs 26:24-26: Honeyed lips conceal a hateful heart.
Psalm 64:2-6: The plots of evildoers against the righteous.

translationNotes.term: Addition B: The edict of Artaxerxes
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἀντίγραφον τῆς ἐπιστολῆς (antigraphon tēs epistolēs, 'copy of the letter'); LXX expansion not present in the Hebrew text.
translationNotes.note: Addition B preserves what later tradition supplied as the actual text of Haman's decree, framed as royal propaganda; it dresses bloodthirsty intent in the language of imperial reasonableness.

stories.keyTakeaway: Addition B records the supposed text of Haman's royal letter; Artaxerxes claims to act for the empire's peace while authorizing the slaughter of the Jewish people on a single day in Adar.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 7
summaryBullets: So the king and Haman went in to drink with the queen. (7:1).

And the second day, as they were drinking wine, the king said, “What is it, Queen Esther? What is your petition, and what is your request? It shall be granted to you, even to half of my kingdom.” (7:2).
She answered and said, “If I have found favor with the king, let my life be granted me at my petition and my people at my request. (7:3).

For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, plundered, and made slaves—we and our children—male and female slaves. I took no heed, but now our adversary brings shame on the king’s court.” (7:4).
Then the king said, “Who is the person who would dare to do this thing?” (7:5).
Esther said, “Our enemy is this evil man Haman!” At this, Haman was terrified in the presence of the king and queen. (7:6).
The king rose from the banquet and went into the garden, and Haman began to beg for his life from the queen, for he saw that he was in serious trouble. (7:7).

When the king returned from the garden, Haman had thrown himself on the couch, pleading with the queen. The king said, “Will you dare even assault my wife in my own house?” Haman, when he heard, turned away his face. (7:8).

Then Bugathan, one of the eunuchs, said to the king, “Look, Haman has even prepared a pole for Mordecai, who gave information of concern to the king; it is standing at Haman’s house, a pole fifty cubits high.” So the king said, “Let Haman be executed on that.” (7:9).
So Haman was hung on the pole that had been prepared for Mordecai. With that the anger of the king abated. (7:10).
crossRefs: Psalm 7:15-16: The wicked falls into the pit he dug.
Proverbs 26:27: He who digs a pit will fall into it.
Esther 9:25: Haman's plot returns upon his own head.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ξύλον (xylon, 'wood, pole'); Hebrew: עֵץ (ʿētz, 'tree, gallows').
translationNotes.note: Persian execution used a tall wooden stake on which the condemned was impaled, not the later Roman gallows; the symbolic reversal places Haman on the very stake he prepared for Mordecai.

stories.keyTakeaway: At Esther's second banquet she exposes Haman as the enemy who has bought her people's destruction; the king, returning from the garden in fury, orders Haman hanged on the very pole he prepared for Mordecai.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 8
summaryBullets: When Mordecai learned of all that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and sprinkled himself with ashes; then he rushed through the street of the city, shouting loudly: “An innocent nation is being destroyed!” (8:1).
He got as far as the king’s gate, and there he stopped, because no one was allowed to enter the courtyard clothed in sackcloth and ashes. (8:2).
And in every province where the letter had been posted there was crying, lamentation, and great mourning among the Jews, and they put on sackcloth and ashes. (8:3).

When the queen’s maids and eunuchs came and told her, she was deeply troubled by what she heard had happened and sent instructions to clothe Mordecai and to remove his sackcloth, but he would not consent. (8:4).
Then Esther summoned Hachratheus, the eunuch who attended her, and dispatched him to get accurate information for her from Mordecai. (8:5).
So Mordecai told him what had happened and about the promise that Haman had promised the king: ten thousand talents for the royal treasury to bring about the destruction of the Jews. (8:7).

He also gave him a copy of what had been posted in Susa for their destruction, to show to Esther, and he told him to charge her to go in to the king and plead for his favor in behalf of the people. “Remember,” he said, “the days when you were an ordinary person, being brought up under my care, for Haman, who is second to the king, has spoken against us and demands our death. Call upon the Lord; then speak to the king in our behalf and save us from death.” (8:8).
Hachratheus went in and told her all these things. (8:9).
And Esther said to him, “Go to Mordecai and say: (8:10).

All nations of the realm know that if any man or woman goes to the king inside the inner court without being called, there is no escape for that person. Only the one to whom the king stretches out the golden scepter is safe—and it is now thirty days since I myself was called to go to the king.” (8:11).
So Hachratheus delivered Esther’s entire message to Mordecai, (8:12).
and then Mordecai said to Hachratheus, “Go and say to her: Esther, do not say to yourself that you alone among all the Jews in the realm will escape alive. (8:13).

For if you take no heed at such a time as this, help and protection will come to the Jews from another quarter, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows whether it was not for such a time as this that you were made queen?” (8:14).
Then Esther gave the messenger this answer to take back to Mordecai: (8:15).

“Go and gather the Jews who are in Susa and fast on my behalf; for three days and nights do not eat or drink, and my maids and I will also go without food. After that I will go to the king, contrary to the law, even if I must die.” (8:16).
So Mordecai went away and did what Esther had told him to do. (8:17).
crossRefs: Exodus 17:9–14: Israel defends against Amalek.
Isaiah 54:17: No weapon formed shall prosper.
Romans 8:31: If God is for us, who can be against us?

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: גְּזֵרָה (gəzērāh, 'decree'), Greek: διάταγμα (diátagma), Aramaic: גזרתא (gəzerātā)
translationNotes.note: An official royal decree, written and sealed, considered irrevocable in Persian law.

stories.keyTakeaway: Mordecai’s counter-edict reverses Haman’s plot, bringing relief and honor to the Jews.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 9
summaryBullets: When the decree had been posted and the Jews throughout the empire had heard, they put on sackcloth and ashes, fasted with their families, and pleaded with the God of their ancestors. (9:1).
Mordecai also remembered all that the Lord had done, and he resolved to call upon him with fasting and weeping for the deliverance of his people. (9:2).
He went out from the king's gate and put off his royal garments, covered his head with ashes, and prostrated himself on the ground. (9:3).
He set his face toward the Most High and stretched out his hands, saying within his heart that the God of Israel had not abandoned the seed of Abraham. (9:4).
All night he kept watch in supplication, denying himself food and water until he should hear an answer. (9:5).
And every Jew in Susa fasted with him, the men, women, and children pouring out their souls before the Lord. (9:6).
Then Mordecai lifted up his voice, and his prayer rose up before the throne of God. (9:7).
Then Mordecai prayed to the Lord, calling to remembrance all the works of the Lord. (9:8).
He said, “O Lord, Lord, King of all powers, for the universe is in your power and there is no one who can oppose you when it is your will to save Israel, (9:9).
for you have made heaven and earth and every wonderful thing under heaven. (9:10).
You are Lord of all, and there is no one who can resist you, the Lord. (9:11).
You know all things; you know, O Lord, that it was not in insolence or pride or for any love of glory that I did this and refused to bow down to this proud Haman, (9:12).
for I would have been willing to kiss the soles of his feet to save Israel! (9:13).
But I did this so that I might not set human glory above the glory of God, and I will not bow down to anyone but you, who are my Lord, and I will not do these things in pride. (9:14).

And now, O Lord God and King, God of Abraham, spare your people, for the eyes of our foes are upon us to annihilate us, and they desire to destroy the inheritance that has been yours from the beginning. (9:15).
Do not neglect your portion, which you redeemed for yourself out of the land of Egypt. (9:16).
Hear my prayer and have mercy upon your inheritance; turn our mourning into feasting that we may live and sing praise to your name, O Lord; do not destroy the lips of those who praise you.” (9:17).
And all Israel cried out with all their might, for their death was before their eyes. (9:18).
crossRefs: Daniel 9:3-19: Daniel's prayer of fasting and confession.
Exodus 32:11-13: Moses appeals to God's covenant with the patriarchs.
Psalm 79:9-10: Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name.

translationNotes.original: Greek: προσευχὴ Μαρδοχαίου (proseuchē Mardochaiou); an LXX expansion preserved only in the Greek tradition.
translationNotes.note: Addition C inserts a theological prayer absent from the Hebrew Esther, giving Mordecai's refusal to bow to Haman a religious motive: he would not place human glory above God's.

stories.keyTakeaway: While the Jews fast across the empire, Mordecai goes apart to pray, confessing that his refusal to bow to Haman was not pride but loyalty to God alone; he begs the Lord to spare his people for the sake of the covenant.

stories.title: 👑 Esther (Greek) 10
summaryBullets: Then Queen Esther, seized with mortal anguish, fled to the Lord. (10:1).

She took off the garments of her honor and put on the garments of distress and mourning, and instead of costly perfumes she covered her head with ashes and dung, and she utterly humbled her body; every part that she loved to adorn she covered with her tangled hair. (10:2).
She prayed to the Lord God of Israel and said: “O my Lord, you alone are our king; help me, who am alone and have no helper but you, (10:3).
for my danger is in my hand. (10:4).

Ever since I was born I have heard in the tribe of my family that you, O Lord, took Israel out of all the nations and our ancestors from among all their forebears for an everlasting inheritance and that you did for them all that you said. (10:5).
And now we have sinned before you, and you have delivered us into the hands of our enemies (10:6).
because we glorified their gods. You are righteous, O Lord! (10:7).
And now they are not satisfied that we are in bitter slavery, but they have set their hands on the hands of their idols (10:8).
to abolish what your mouth has ordained and to destroy your inheritance, to stop the mouths of those who praise you and to quench your altar and the glory of your house, (10:9).
to open the mouths of the nations for the praise of vain idols and to magnify forever a mortal king. (10:10).
“O Lord, do not surrender your scepter to what has no being, and do not let them laugh at our downfall, but turn their plan against them and make an example of him who began this against us. (10:11).
Remember, O Lord; make yourself known in this time of our affliction and give me courage, O King of the gods and Master of all dominion! (10:12).
Put eloquent speech in my mouth before the lion and turn his heart to hate the man who is fighting against us, so that there may be an end of him and those who agree with him. (10:13).
Save us by your hand, and help me, who am alone and have no helper but you, O Lord. You have knowledge of all things, (10:14).
and you know that I hate the splendor of the wicked and abhor the bed of the uncircumcised and of any alien. (10:15).

You know my necessity, that I abhor the sign of my proud position, which is upon my head on days when I appear in public. I abhor it like a filthy rag, and I do not wear it on the days when I am at leisure. (10:16).
And your servant has not eaten at Haman's table, and I have not honored the king's feast or drunk the wine of libations. (10:17).
Your servant has had no joy since the day that I was brought here until now, except in you, O Lord God of Abraham. (10:18).
O God, whose might is over all, hear the voice of the despairing, and save us from the hands of evildoers. And save me from my fear!” (10:19).
crossRefs: Daniel 1:8: Refusing to defile oneself with the king's food.
Psalm 22:11: There is none to help; God alone is hope.
Esther 4:16: If I perish, I perish.

translationNotes.original: Greek: προσευχὴ Ἐσθήρ (proseuchē Esthēr); LXX expansion paired with the prayer of Mordecai.
translationNotes.note: Esther's prayer protests her piety: she has not enjoyed the splendor of the Persian court, has not eaten at Haman's table, and has not drunk the wine of pagan libations; the Greek shapes her as a Daniel-figure inside the harem.

stories.keyTakeaway: Esther strips off her royal garments, covers herself in ashes, and pours out her prayer to the God of Abraham; she confesses that the throne disgusts her, that she has refused Haman's table and the king's libations, and she begs God for courage before the lion.
